name: HumanEval / HumanEval+
authors: Chen et al. (OpenAI) 2021; Liu et al. 2023
format: 164 Python function stubs with docstrings; model must produce correct function body; HumanEval+ adds 80× more unit tests per problem
dataset_source: Hand-authored by OpenAI engineers; HumanEval+ tests generated via mutation and LLM augmentation
known_limitations: HumanEval is acknowledged as saturated (Claude 4 achieves ~90%+); single-file Python only; no library calls; all problems solvable without real-world context; HumanEval+ mitigates but does not eliminate saturation
contamination_risk: High — 164 problems are widely memorised; HumanEval+ reduces but cannot eliminate contamination
quality_notes: Coherence 4: tasks are internally consistent but narrow in scope. Accuracy 4: HumanEval+ substantially reduces false positives from weak unit tests. Clarity 5: problem specifications are unambiguous. Relevance 3: isolated function completion does not reflect real software development workflows. Efficiency 5: fully automated; cheap to run at scale.

name: MBPP / MBPP+ (EvalPlus)
authors: Austin et al. (Google) 2021; Liu et al. 2023
format: ~974 Python problems with natural language description; model generates function or script; MBPP+ adds augmented test cases
dataset_source: Crowdsourced from Amazon Mechanical Turk; MBPP+ test augmentation via EvalPlus pipeline
known_limitations: Crowdsourced problems have noisier quality than hand-authored HumanEval; some problems have ambiguous specifications; MBPP+ sanitised subset (399) is smaller; entry-level difficulty means frontier models approach ceiling
contamination_risk: High — widely published; training data contamination highly probable for most frontier models
quality_notes: Coherence 3: crowdsourced origin means some inconsistency in problem style and test coverage. Accuracy 4: MBPP+ improves test rigour substantially. Clarity 4: most problems are clear but some ambiguity exists from crowdsourcing. Relevance 3: similar to HumanEval — isolated scripting rather than real engineering tasks. Efficiency 5: fully automated pass@k evaluation.

name: SWE-bench Verified
citation_count: >1200 (SWE-bench); cited as standard in >50 technical reports
format: Model receives GitHub issue description and must produce a code patch resolving the issue; evaluated on whether repo test suite passes after patch application
dataset_source: Real GitHub issues from 12 popular Python repositories (scikit-learn / sympy / requests / flask etc.); human-verified subset confirmed as solvable and unambiguous
human_involvement: Yes — human verification of 500-issue Verified subset; no human in evaluation loop
known_limitations: Requires running full repository test suite — expensive compute; Python only; repository-specific context may not generalise; human verification was cross-sectional (April 2024 snapshot of repos)
contamination_risk: Medium — issues are real and specific; reproduction is harder than MBPP but contamination through GitHub scraping is possible for models trained post-2023
update_frequency: Static (Verified); Full benchmark maintained by authors
quality_notes: Coherence 5: tasks are internally consistent — resolve issue so tests pass is a clear objective. Accuracy 5: binary pass/fail via real test suites is the most accurate evaluation signal in C02. Clarity 4: issue descriptions vary in quality (real GitHub issues); some ambiguity inherent. Relevance 5: the most realistic code benchmark available; directly mirrors real engineering work. Efficiency 3: high compute cost; requires full repo environment per issue; not trivial to run locally.

name: LiveCodeBench
format: Multi-task: code generation / self-repair / test output prediction / code execution reasoning; problems drawn monthly from LeetCode / AtCoder / Codeforces post training cutoff
dataset_size: ~2000+ problems as of April 2026 (continuously growing); monthly additions
dataset_source: Competitive programming problems published after training cutoffs of major models; manually collected and verified
known_limitations: Competitive programming style may not reflect industry software engineering; monthly refresh means benchmark evolves and historical comparisons require version control; coverage limited to algorithmic domains
contamination_risk: Low — by design; problems post-date training data; ongoing contamination risk increases over time as models retrain
quality_notes: Coherence 5: consistent task format with clear sub-task boundaries. Accuracy 5: automated pass/fail against verified test cases. Clarity 5: problems are competition-quality with clear specifications. Relevance 4: highly relevant for algorithmic coding; moderate for real engineering tasks. Efficiency 4: automated but requires monthly maintenance; versioning adds operational complexity.

name: BigCodeBench (Hard)
format: Model must write Python code calling real library APIs (NumPy / Pandas / scikit-learn / requests / etc.) to complete multi-step tasks; Hard subset = 148 most challenging items
dataset_size: 1140 total tasks (BCB Complete); 148 (BCB Hard); 33 (BCB Instruct Hard)
dataset_source: Semi-automated construction with human verification; tasks seeded from realistic programming scenarios requiring library knowledge
evaluation_metric: pass@1; calibrated difficulty against human expert performance
known_limitations: 148 items in Hard subset is small; Python-only; library versions evolve meaning some tasks may become outdated; LLM-generated test cases in construction pipeline may introduce subtle errors
contamination_risk: Medium — fewer problems but less widely publicised than HumanEval; library-specific tasks harder to memorise
quality_notes: Coherence 4: library integration tasks are coherent and internally consistent. Accuracy 4: real test execution but smaller test suite per item than EvalPlus. Clarity 4: task descriptions clear but require library knowledge to interpret. Relevance 5: measures exactly the real-world skill of using existing libraries — the most common real engineering activity. Efficiency 4: automated but requires library environments; slightly higher setup cost than HumanEval.

name: IFEval
format: 541 prompts each with 1–3 verifiable constraints (e.g. 'respond in exactly 3 paragraphs' / 'include the word elephant' / 'end with a question mark'); model response evaluated against constraints programmatically
dataset_source: Manually authored by researchers with explicit verifiability criterion for each constraint
evaluation_metric: Prompt-level accuracy (all constraints met) and instruction-level accuracy (each constraint individually); both strict and loose variants
known_limitations: Short prompt focus (few sentences to a paragraph) not long-form writing; 25 constraint types cover formatting/length/keywords but not writing quality/style/creativity; a model could satisfy all constraints while producing poor-quality text; ceiling effect emerging on frontier models as of 2025
contamination_risk: Low — prompts are numerous (541) and constraints are diverse; programmatic evaluation reduces gaming
quality_notes: Coherence 4: constraint types are well-defined but the benchmark reduces writing to constraint-satisfaction rather than quality. Accuracy 5: programmatic verification is highly reliable for verifiable constraints. Clarity 5: instructions and constraints are unambiguous. Relevance 3: real-world writing tasks require quality and style not just constraint compliance; IFEval is a proxy not a direct measure of C01. Efficiency 5: fully automated; fast to run.

name: WritingBench
venue: NeurIPS 2025 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track); arXiv forthcoming
format: 1239 multi-domain writing prompts; model generates full text response; evaluated by a query-dependent critic model that selects evaluation criteria based on the specific writing task
domain: Creative / persuasive / informative / technical / professional writing
dataset_size: 1239 queries across 6 primary domains and 100 subdomains
dataset_source: Curated by researchers using a taxonomy of writing tasks; prompts designed to span real-world writing scenarios
evaluation_metric: Query-dependent critic model scoring; domain-specific rubrics; human calibration of critic model
human_involvement: Partial — human calibration of critic model; no human in primary evaluation loop
known_limitations: LLM-as-judge reliability depends on judge model quality; critic model may share biases with evaluated models; citation count low as of April 2026 (new publication); no frontier model has benchmarked against it (gap evidence)
contamination_risk: Low — large diverse prompt set; judge-based evaluation resists simple memorisation
quality_notes: Coherence 5: taxonomy-driven construction ensures coverage across writing types is principled. Accuracy 4: query-dependent critic is well-designed but LLM judges have known reliability limits. Clarity 4: writing prompts are clear but open-ended by design making evaluation inherently subjective. Relevance 5: directly measures real-world writing tasks at realistic length and complexity. Efficiency 3: LLM-as-judge evaluation adds latency and cost; critic model must be run per prompt.

name: EQ-Bench Creative Writing v3 + Longform Writing
task_type: Open-ended creative writing with LLM-as-judge + Elo
format: EQ-Bench Creative Writing: short creative writing prompts evaluated on 4 dimensions (emotional authenticity / narrative craft / character voice / stylistic originality); Longform Writing: longer creative pieces; Elo-based ranking across models via pairwise comparison
dataset_size: ~60 prompts (creative writing component); ~20 (longform); Elo computed over >10000 pairwise battles
dataset_source: Hand-authored creative writing prompts; Elo accumulated from community submissions
evaluation_metric: Elo score from pairwise LLM judge comparisons; rubric scores on 4 dimensions (1–10 scale)
human_involvement: Partial — human-designed rubric; LLM-judged pairwise comparisons; no human judges in primary loop
known_limitations: Small prompt set (60 items) limits statistical reliability; single-researcher maintenance creates bus-factor risk; judge model biases may favour certain writing styles; Elo accumulation means earlier and newer models compared under different judge versions
contamination_risk: Low — creative prompts are diverse and open-ended; Elo-based evaluation resists gaming
quality_notes: Coherence 4: rubric dimensions are principled but small prompt set limits generalisability. Accuracy 3: LLM-judged Elo has reproducibility concerns; judge model version changes can shift rankings. Clarity 4: prompts are creative by design (inherently open); rubric dimensions are clear. Relevance 5: measures exactly what real creative writing quality requires — style, voice, authenticity. Efficiency 3: Elo accumulation is slow; running the full benchmark requires many pairwise comparisons.

name: HelloBench / LongBench-Write
authors: Que et al. (HelloBench) 2024; Bai et al. (LongBench-Write) 2024
task_type: Long-form text generation with multi-dimensional scoring
format: HelloBench: diverse long-form writing tasks (story / essay / email / report / etc.) with task-specific evaluation dimensions; LongBench-Write: 6 fixed dimensions across document types (relevance / coherence / fluency / length adherence / instruction following / creativity)
domain: Long-form writing across professional and creative contexts
dataset_source: Curated by researchers; prompts represent real-world long-form writing scenarios
evaluation_metric: HelloBench: task-specific automated + LLM-judge scoring; LongBench-Write: GPT-4-judged rubric scoring on 6 dimensions
human_involvement: Partial — LLM judges; no human in primary loop
known_limitations: Small datasets; LLM judge reliability; limited to text-only outputs (no code/structured data in writing tasks); evaluation dimensions in LongBench-Write are fixed and may not suit all task types
contamination_risk: Low — diverse tasks and open-ended outputs
quality_notes: Coherence 4: task taxonomy is principled; fixed dimensions in LongBench-Write ensure consistency. Accuracy 3: LLM judge reliability is the main limitation; task-specific dimensions in HelloBench improve over generic rubrics. Clarity 4: prompts are clear and realistic. Relevance 5: directly addresses long-form writing — the dominant real-world C01 use case. Efficiency 3: LLM judge adds cost; small dataset partially compensates.

name: MathDial
format: 2900 student–tutor dialogues grounded in GSM8K math problems; model plays the tutor role responding to a student message in context; evaluated on pedagogical quality not answer correctness
dataset_source: Collected via paid crowdworker tutors interacting with a simulated student making errors on GSM8K problems; human-authored responses
evaluation_metric: Automatic: next-turn prediction accuracy vs. human reference; Manual: rubric-based pedagogical quality ratings on subset
human_involvement: Partial — human-authored reference responses; human ratings on validation subset
known_limitations: Restricted to GSM8K problem domain (elementary arithmetic); tutors are crowdworkers not trained educators — quality varies; evaluation via reference-matching penalises equally valid alternative pedagogical responses; English-only
contamination_risk: Low — multi-turn dialogue grounded in specific problem instances; hard to memorise
quality_notes: Coherence 4: consistent student-tutor format grounded in verifiable maths problems. Accuracy 3: reference-based evaluation penalises valid alternative tutoring approaches; human ratings on validation subset are the gold standard but expensive to extend. Clarity 4: task setup is clear; tutoring objective is well-specified. Relevance 5: directly measures tutoring — the C04 use case documented in Handa et al. Efficiency 3: reference-based evaluation is noisy; human rating is expensive; automatic metrics are weak proxies.

name: MRBench
format: 192 tutoring dialogues × 7 LLM tutors × 8 pedagogical dimensions; evaluates AI tutor responses against expert-annotated ideal responses using Desired Annotation Match Rate (DAMR) metric
domain: Mathematics education / pedagogical quality across multiple dimensions
dataset_size: 192 dialogues; 7 tutors evaluated; 8 dimensions = 10752 evaluation instances
dataset_source: Expert-annotated pedagogical rubric; 192 dialogues drawn from real student–tutor interactions; expert educators provided annotations
evaluation_metric: Desired Annotation Match Rate (DAMR) — proportion of expert-desired pedagogical behaviours exhibited by model tutor
human_involvement: Yes — expert educators annotated all 192 dialogues across 8 dimensions
known_limitations: Small dataset (192 dialogues); expert annotation is expensive limiting scalability; 8 dimensions were selected by researchers and may not be exhaustive; English-only; maths domain only
contamination_risk: Low — expert annotations are dialogue-specific; small set limits memorisation risk
quality_notes: Coherence 5: 8 dimensions provide a comprehensive and principled pedagogical taxonomy. Accuracy 5: expert annotations are the most reliable ground truth available for pedagogical quality. Clarity 4: DAMR metric is well-defined; 8 dimensions are clearly operationalised. Relevance 5: multi-dimensional pedagogy measurement is exactly what C04 requires. Efficiency 2: expert annotation is expensive; 192 dialogues is small; scaling is the primary limitation.

name: MathTutorBench
format: 7 pedagogical tasks: socratic questioning / mistake localisation / feedback generation / hint provision / problem reformulation / pedagogy plan following / student error explanation; each task evaluated separately
domain: Mathematics education across multiple pedagogical sub-skills
dataset_size: Varies by task; ~500–2000 items per task; full benchmark ~7000 evaluation instances
dataset_source: Combination of existing tutoring datasets (MathDial / Bridge / CIMA etc.) and newly constructed items; pedagogy reward model trained on expert preferences
evaluation_metric: Pedagogy reward model score (primary); task-specific automatic metrics (secondary)
human_involvement: Partial — pedagogy reward model trained on human expert preferences; no human in primary evaluation loop
secondary_capabilities: C03 (maths knowledge) / C05 (feedback generation task overlaps critique)
known_limitations: Reward model may amplify biases of training preferences; 7 tasks are independently evaluated making aggregate interpretation complex; reward model requires periodic retraining as frontier model capabilities shift; primarily English-language maths
contamination_risk: Low — reward model evaluation of open-ended tutoring responses is hard to game
quality_notes: Coherence 5: 7 tasks cover the full range of tutoring sub-skills in a principled framework. Accuracy 4: reward model is well-calibrated against expert preferences but introduces model-in-loop reliability concerns. Clarity 4: task definitions are clear; reward model training procedure is documented. Relevance 5: most comprehensive C04 benchmark available; public leaderboard enables community comparison. Efficiency 3: 7 tasks + reward model evaluation adds overhead; not trivial to run locally.

name: MMLU / MMLU-Pro
authors: Hendrycks et al. (MMLU) 2020; Wang et al. (MMLU-Pro) 2024
format: 57-subject multiple-choice QA (MMLU; 4 options); 14-subject harder MCQ with 10 options and more reasoning-intensive questions (MMLU-Pro); model selects answer from options
domain: Academic knowledge across STEM / humanities / social sciences / professional domains
dataset_source: MMLU: collected from internet resources and standardised tests; MMLU-Pro: filtered and augmented from MMLU with harder items and increased option count
human_involvement: No — automated scoring against answer key
secondary_capabilities: C04 (academic knowledge questions overlap tutoring domain)
known_limitations: MMLU is broadly saturated (frontier models >88%); multiple-choice format gameable by elimination/position bias; knowledge cutoff issues; MMLU-Pro partially addresses saturation but also approaching ceiling; questions test recall not application or reasoning
contamination_risk: High (MMLU) — 14000 widely published questions; likely in training data of most frontier models. Medium (MMLU-Pro) — harder items and 10-option format reduce but do not eliminate contamination risk
quality_notes: Coherence 3: diverse subjects are useful but MCQ format creates artificial uniformity across very different knowledge types. Accuracy 4: MMLU-Pro's harder items and 10-option format improve over MMLU but MCQ format limits measurement of genuine understanding. Clarity 4: questions are generally clear; some items have acknowledged quality issues. Relevance 3: tests academic knowledge recall not real-world information-seeking behaviour; MMLU-Pro improves but gap remains. Efficiency 5: fully automated; extremely fast to evaluate; widely supported across evaluation frameworks.

name: GPQA Diamond
format: 448-item Diamond subset of GPQA; graduate-level questions in biology / chemistry / physics; model selects one of 4 options; questions verified to be unsolvable by search (require genuine expert reasoning)
dataset_source: Hand-authored by domain experts (PhD students and researchers); each question verified by at least one other expert; Google search validation to ensure non-googleability
human_involvement: Yes — expert authorship and peer validation of all questions; no human in evaluation loop
known_limitations: 448 items is small for statistical reliability at aggregate level; English-only; STEM-only (no humanities / social science / professional knowledge); gated access may limit replication; as frontier models approach ceiling the benchmark will saturate
contamination_risk: Low — gated access prevents wide distribution; expert-level questions are harder to memorise; contamination is limited but access controls must be maintained
quality_notes: Coherence 5: questions are uniformly expert-validated and designed to test genuine reasoning not recall. Accuracy 5: expert validation with cross-verification is the strongest available ground truth for factual reasoning benchmarks. Clarity 5: questions are precisely worded by domain experts. Relevance 4: graduate STEM reasoning is important but does not cover professional advisory or social science knowledge domains. Efficiency 4: small set makes individual runs fast; gated access adds operational friction.

name: TriviaQA / Natural Questions
authors: Joshi et al. (TriviaQA) 2017; Kwiatkowski et al. (NQ) 2019
format: TriviaQA: 95k trivia question-answer pairs with evidence documents; NQ: 300k Google search queries with Wikipedia long and short answer spans; model produces a free-text short answer
dataset_size: 95k (TriviaQA); 300k (NQ); typically evaluated on dev/test subsets of ~10–20k
dataset_source: TriviaQA: crowdsourced from trivia enthusiasts with Wikipedia/web evidence; NQ: Google search logs with Wikipedia answer annotations
evaluation_metric: Exact match (EM) and F1 against answer strings; TriviaQA also uses evidence-based filtering
known_limitations: Both benchmarks are old (2017/2019) and widely saturated (frontier models >85% EM on TriviaQA); simple short-form answers do not capture the complexity of real information-seeking; knowledge cutoff issues for questions about recent events
contamination_risk: High — both are very widely published and almost certainly in training data of frontier models; contamination is the primary reliability concern
quality_notes: Coherence 3: format consistency is good but short-answer QA is a narrow proxy for real information retrieval. Accuracy 3: string-match metrics (EM/F1) are noisy — paraphrases counted wrong; factual currency degrades over time. Clarity 4: questions are clear and natural. Relevance 4: represent real user search/lookup behaviour but at low complexity vs. actual advisory tasks. Efficiency 5: fully automated; fast; widely supported.

name: SimpleQA / FACTS Grounding
authors: Wei et al. (OpenAI — SimpleQA); Jacovi et al. (Google — FACTS)
venue: SimpleQA: OpenAI technical blog 2024; FACTS: arXiv 2024 / Google
format: SimpleQA: 4326 questions each with a single unambiguous correct answer (often a proper noun or number); FACTS Grounding: 860 grounding tasks where model must produce responses faithful to provided source documents
dataset_source: SimpleQA: curated by OpenAI with expert verification of ground truth uniqueness; FACTS: curated by Google with document-answer pairs designed to test faithful grounding
evaluation_metric: SimpleQA: accuracy (% exactly correct); FACTS: grounding score (proportion of response claims supported by document)
human_involvement: Partial — expert verification of ground truth (SimpleQA); document-grounding labels (FACTS); no human in evaluation loop
known_limitations: SimpleQA tests only knowledge recall of unambiguous facts — does not measure reasoning or advisory capability; FACTS tests grounding against provided context but real-world advisory often involves synthesising multiple sources; both are new (2024) and adoption is still spreading
contamination_risk: Low (SimpleQA) — 4326 diverse unambiguous facts are harder to memorise than MMLU MCQs; Low (FACTS) — grounding tasks depend on provided documents not training data
quality_notes: Coherence 4: both benchmarks have clear and consistent evaluation objectives. Accuracy 5: unambiguous ground truth (SimpleQA) and document-grounding labels (FACTS) provide high reliability. Clarity 5: questions and tasks are precisely specified. Relevance 4: hallucination measurement is directly relevant to C03 advisory tasks but these benchmarks cover only a subset of what advisory capability requires. Efficiency 4: automated; moderate dataset sizes; FACTS requires document processing overhead.

name: CriticBench (Tsinghua)
format: Model receives a solution or output and must: (a) critique it by identifying errors and (b) generate a corrected version; 15 datasets spanning math / commonsense / symbolic reasoning / code / algorithmic problems
domain: Critique and correction across multiple reasoning domains
dataset_size: 3825 instances across 15 datasets (5 domains × 3 datasets each)
dataset_source: Aggregated from existing datasets (GSM8K / CommonsenseQA / MATH / HumanEval / etc.) with error injection and human-verified critique-correction pairs
evaluation_metric: Critique quality (binary: does critique correctly identify error?); correction accuracy (does corrected output solve the problem?); composite CriticBench score
human_involvement: Partial — human verification of error injection and critique-correction pairs
secondary_capabilities: C02 (code critique) / C03 (reasoning critique) / C04 (math critique)
known_limitations: Critique-and-correct format measures error-identification capability but not the full range of feedback (style / tone / structure / argumentation that real review involves); primarily STEM domains; no natural language prose critique tasks (essay feedback); no frontier model reports CriticBench results — gap evidence
contamination_risk: Low — critique targets specific injected errors in specific instances; hard to memorise; diverse domains reduce contamination risk
quality_notes: Coherence 5: five-domain taxonomy with three datasets per domain is principled and internally consistent. Accuracy 4: binary critique correctness is reliable for STEM domains; correction accuracy leverages existing benchmark ground truths. Clarity 4: critique-and-correct format is well-defined; evaluation protocol is documented. Relevance 4: measures a real and important C05 sub-skill but misses prose review / editorial feedback / style critique. Efficiency 4: automated evaluation against existing benchmarks; LLM-generated critiques are cheap to produce.

name: Auto-J + Shepherd + MetaCritique (grouped)
authors: Li et al. (Auto-J) 2024; Wang et al. (Shepherd) 2023; Sun et al. (MetaCritique) 2024
task_type: Open-ended critique generation with human-annotated references
format: Auto-J: 4396 critique instances across 58 real-world scenarios including essay feedback / code review / general instruction following; Shepherd: natural language feedback on model outputs with human-written reference feedback; MetaCritique: evaluates the quality of critiques themselves using a meta-evaluation framework
domain: Open-ended critique: essay / code review / general instruction output quality
dataset_size: Auto-J: 4396 instances; Shepherd: ~1000 instances; MetaCritique: varies
dataset_source: Auto-J: human-curated from real LLM outputs in 58 deployment scenarios; Shepherd: human-written feedback on diverse model outputs; MetaCritique: human judgements on critique quality
evaluation_metric: Auto-J: pairwise preference (human-annotated); Shepherd: similarity to human reference feedback (ROUGE/BERTScore + human evaluation); MetaCritique: accuracy of meta-evaluation
human_involvement: Yes — human annotations in all three components; human-authored reference feedback central to evaluation
known_limitations: Three separate benchmarks grouped for coverage — no single unified evaluation protocol; Auto-J's 58 scenarios are diverse but may not cover all C05 sub-tasks; Shepherd's reference-similarity metrics are noisy (paraphrase issue); MetaCritique is small and new; none has cross-lab benchmark adoption
contamination_risk: Low — human-annotated real LLM outputs in diverse scenarios are difficult to memorise; open-ended critique is hard to game
quality_notes: Coherence 4: three complementary benchmarks together cover open-ended critique well but lack a unified protocol. Accuracy 4: human annotations are reliable but ROUGE/BERTScore metrics for Shepherd are noisy. Clarity 3: three-benchmark grouping creates complexity; evaluation protocols differ across components; researchers must navigate multiple frameworks. Relevance 5: Auto-J's 58 real-world scenarios directly reflect deployed LLM critique use cases; the most ecologically valid C05 coverage available. Efficiency 3: human annotation cost is high; diverse protocols increase operational complexity.
